PREFACE
This Code constitutes a complete recodification of the ordinances of the City of a general and permanent nature.
Source materials used in the preparation of the Code were the 1963 Code, as supplemented through 1983, and ordinances subsequently adopted by the Council. The source of each section is included in the history note appearing in parentheses at the end thereof. The absence of such a note indicates that the section is new and was adopted for the first time with the adoption of the Code. By use of the Comparative Tables appearing in the back of this volume, the reader can locate any section of the 1963 Code, as supplemented, and any subsequent ordinance included herein.
The chapters of the Code have been conveniently arranged in alphabetical order and the various sections within each chapter have been catchlined to facilitate usage. Footnotes which tie related sections of the Code together and which refer to relevant state laws have been included. A table listing the state law citations and setting forth their location within the Code is included at the back of this volume.
Numbering System
The numbering system used in this Code is the same system used in many state and municipal codes. Each section number consists of two component parts separated by a dash, the figure before the dash referring to the chapter number and the figure after the dash referring to the position of the section within the chapter. Thus, the first section of Chapter 9 is numbered 9-1 and the tenth section of Chapter 4 is 4-10. Under this system, each section is identified with its chapter and at the same time new sections or even whole chapters can be inserted in their proper place simply by using the decimal system for amendments. By way of illustration: If new material consisting of three sections that would logically come between sections 3-2 and 3-3 is desired to be added, such new sections would be numbered 3-2.1, 3-2.2 and 3-2.3 respectively. New chapters may be included in the same manner. If the new material is to be included between Chapters 6 and 7, it will be designated as Chapter 6.5. Care should be taken that the alphabetical arrangement of chapters is maintained when including new chapters. New articles and new divisions may be included in the same way or, in the case of articles, may be placed at the end of the chapter embracing the subject, and, in the case of divisions, may be placed at the end of the article embracing the subject, the next successive number being assigned to the article or division.
Indices
The indices of the Code have been prepared with the greatest of care. Each particular item has been placed under several headings, some of the headings being couched in lay phraseology, others in legal terminology, and still others in language generally used by municipal officials and employees. There are numerous cross references within the indices themselves which stand as guideposts to direct the user to the particular item in which he is interested.
Looseleaf Supplements
A special feature of this Code to which the attention of the user is especially directed is the looseleaf system of binding and supplemental servicing for the Code. With this system, the Code will be kept up-to-date periodically. Upon the final passage of amendatory ordinances, they will be properly edited and the appropriate page or pages affected will be reprinted. These new pages will be distributed to holders of copies of the Code, with instructions for the manner of inserting the new pages and deleting the obsolete pages. Each such amendment, when incorporated into this Code, may be cited as a part hereof.
The successful maintenance of this Code up-to-date at all times will depend largely upon the holder of the volume. As revised sheets are received, it will then become the responsibility of the holder to have the amendments inserted according to the attached instructions. It is strongly recommended by the publishers that all such amendments be inserted immediately upon receipt to avoid misplacing them and, in addition, that all deleted pages be saved and filed for historical reference purposes.
Acknowledgments
The publication of this Code was under direct supervision of B. Meade White of the Municipal Code Corporation, Tallahassee, Florida. Credit is gratefully given to the other members of the publisher's staff for their sincere interest and able assistance through the project.
The publishers are most grateful to the officials of the city for their cooperation and assistance during the progress of the work on this Code. It is hoped that their efforts and those of the publishers have resulted in a Code of Ordinances which will make the active law of the City readily accessible to all citizens and which will be a valuable tool in the day-to-day administration of the City's affairs.

ORDINANCE 2002-21
AN ORDINANCE TO RE-ADOPT THE CODE OF ORDINANCES, CITY OF COLLEGE PARK, GEORGIA, TO PROVIDE TO PROVIDE SEVERABILITY; TO PROVIDE FOR REPEAL OF CONFLICTING ORDINANCES; TO PROVIDE FOR OTHER LAWFUL PURPOSES.
WHEREAS, the Constitution of the State of Georgia, Article IX, Section II, Paragraph II authorized the General Assembly to enact statutes granting municipalities in the State of Georgia certain home rule powers; and
WHEREAS, the General Assembly subsequently enacted Section 36-35-3 (a) of the Official Code of Georgia, which authorizes municipalities in the State of Georgia to adopt ordinances; and
WHEREAS, the duly elected governing authority of the City of College Park, Georgia is the Mayor and Council thereof; and
WHEREAS, the governing authority desires to re-adopt the Code of Ordinances, City of College Park, Georgia in its entirety; and
WHEREAS, said re-adoption would benefit the health, safety and welfare of the citizens of the City of College Park by ensuring the existence of an enforceable City Code.
BE IT AND IT IS HEREBY ORDAINED by the Mayor and Council of the City of College Park, Georgia, and by the authority thereof:
Section 1. It is the intention of the governing body, and it is hereby ordained that the "Code of Ordinances, City of College Park," including "Appendix "A," The Zoning Ordinance of the City of College Park" is hereby re-adopted in its entirety in the form as shown on Exhibit "A." Exhibit "A" shall be a public record accessible to members of the public who are, or may be, affected by it, and shall be kept by the City Clerk in the Office of the City Clerk.
Section 2. It is the intention of the governing body, and it is hereby ordained that the "Official Zoning Map," City of College Park, Georgia, present in the council chamber this date and so certified by the Mayor, is hereby re-adopted in its entirety in the form as shown on the attached Exhibit "B." Exhibit "B" shall be a public record accessible to members of the public who are, or may be, affected by it, and shall be kept by the City Clerk in the Office of the City Clerk.
Section 3. The preamble of this Ordinance shall be considered to be and is hereby incorporated by reference as if fully set out herein.
Section 4. This Ordinance shall be codified in a manner consistent with the laws of the State of Georgia and the City of College Park.
Section 5. (a) It is hereby declared to be the intention of the Mayor and Council that all sections, paragraphs, sentences, clauses and phrases of this Ordinance are or were, upon their enactment, believed by the Mayor and Council to be fully valid, enforceable and constitutional.
(b) It is hereby declared to be the intention of the Mayor and council that, to the greatest extent allowed by law, each and every section, paragraph, sentence, clause or phrase of this Ordinance is severable from every other section, paragraph, sentence, clause or phrase of this Ordinance. It is hereby further declared to be the intention of the Mayor and Council that, to the greatest extent allowed by law, no section, paragraph, sentence, clause or phrase of this Ordinance is mutually dependent upon any other section, paragraph, sentence, clause or phrase of this Ordinance.
(c) In the event that any phrase, clause, sentence, paragraph or section of this Ordinance shall, for any reason whatsoever, be declared invalid, unconstitutional or otherwise unenforceable by the valid judgement or decree of any court of competent jurisdiction, it is the express intent of the Mayor and Council that such invalidity, unconstitutionality or unenforceability shall, to the greatest extend allowed by law, not render invalid, unconstitutional or otherwise unenforceable any of the remaining phrases, clauses, sentences, paragraphs and sections of the Ordinance shall remain valid, constitutional, enforceable, and of full force and effect.
Section 6. All ordinances and parts of ordinances in conflict herewith are hereby expressly repealed.
Section 7. Penalties in effect for violations of the Code of Ordinances, City of College Park at the time of the effective date of this Ordinance shall be and are hereby made applicable to this Ordinance and shall remain in full force and effect.
Section 8. The effective date of this Ordinance shall be date of adoption unless otherwise specified herein.

In the construction of this Code, and of all ordinances, the following rules shall be observed, unless such construction would be inconsistent with the manifest intent of the governing body:
City. The terms "the city" and "this city" shall mean the City of College Park, Georgia.
Computation of time. Whenever a notice is required to be given or an act to be done, a certain length of time before any proceeding shall be had, the day on which such notice is given, or such act is done, shall be counted in computing the time, but the day on which such proceeding is to be had shall not be counted.
County. The terms "the county" and "this county" shall mean the County of Fulton or the County of Clayton, or both, whichever is proper in the circumstances.
Delegation of authority. Whenever a provision appears requiring the head of a department or other officer or employee of the city to do the same act or make certain inspections it is to be construed to authorize the head of the department or other officer or employee to designate, delegate and authorize subordinates to perform the required act or make the required inspection unless the terms of the provision or section designate otherwise.
Gender. A word importing one gender shall extend and be applied to the other genders.
Interpretation. In the interpretation and application of any provision of this Code, it shall be held to be the minimum requirements adopted for the promotion of the public health, safety, comfort, convenience and general welfare. Where any provision of the Code imposes greater restrictions upon the subject matter than the general provision imposed by the Code, the provision imposing the greater restriction or regulation shall be deemed to be controlling.
Joint authority. All words giving a joint authority to three (3) or more persons or officers shall be construed as giving such authority to a majority of such persons or officers.
Keeper and proprietor. The words "keeper" and "proprietor" shall mean and include persons, firms, associations, corporations, clubs and partnerships, whether acting by themselves or through a servant, agent or employee.
Mayor, other official, officer or employee. Whenever the word "mayor", or the title of any other official, officer or employee of the city, is used it shall mean the mayor, or such other official, officer or employee of the City of College Park.
Mayor and council, council, city council, governing body. Whenever the term "mayor and council", "council", "city council", or governing body" is used, it shall be construed to mean the mayor and council of the City of College Park.
Month. The word "month" shall mean a calendar month.
Nontechnical and technical words. Words and phrases shall be construed according to the common and approved usage of the language; but technical words and phrases and such others as may have acquired a peculiar and appropriate meaning in law shall be construed and understood according to such meaning.
Number. A word importing the singular number only may extend and be applied to several persons and things as well as to one (1) person and thing.
Oath. The word "oath" shall be construed to include an affirmation in all cases in which, by law, an affirmation may be substituted for an oath, and in such cases the words "swear" and "sworn" shall be equivalent to the words "affirm" and "affirmed".
Or, and. "Or" may be read "and" and "and" may be read "or" if the sense requires it.
Owner. The word "owner," applied to a building or land, shall include any part owner, joint owner, tenant in common, tenant in partnership, joint tenant, or tenant by the entirety, of the whole or of a part of such building or land.
Person. The word "person" shall extend and be applied to associations, clubs, societies, firms, partnerships and bodies politic and corporate as well as to individuals.
Personal property. The term "personal property" shall include every species of property except real property, as herein described.
Preceding, following. The words "preceding" and "following" shall mean next before and next after, respectively.
Premises. Whenever the word "premises" is used it shall mean place or places.
Property. The word "property" shall include real and personal property.
Public place. The term "public place" shall mean any park, cemetery, school yard or open space adjacent thereto, or any area available and/or accessible to the public.
Real property. The term "real property" shall include lands, tenements and hereditaments.
Residence. The term "residence" shall be construed to mean the place adopted by a person as such person's place of habitation, and to which, whenever such person is absent, such person has the intention of returning. When a person eats at one place and sleeps at another, the place where such person sleeps shall be deemed such person's residence.
Seal. The word "seal" shall mean the city seal, the seal of the corporation.
Sidewalk. The word "sidewalk" shall mean any portion of a street between the curb line and the adjacent property line, intended for the use of pedestrians, excluding parkways.
Signature or subscription. The signature or subscription of a person shall include a mark when the person can not write.
State. The terms "the state" and "this state" shall be construed to mean the State of Georgia.
Street. The word "street" shall be construed to embrace streets, avenues, boulevards, roads, alleys, lanes, viaducts and all other public highways in the city.
Tenant, occupant. The words "tenant" or "occupant," applied to a building or land, shall include any person holding a written or oral lease or who occupies the whole or a part of such building or land, either alone or with others.
Tense. Words used in the past or present tense include the future as well as the past and present.
Week. The word "week" shall be construed to mean seven (7) days.
Written or in writing. The terms "written" and "in writing" shall be construed to include any representation of words, letters or figures, whether by printing or otherwise.
Year. The word "year" shall mean a calendar year.
State Law reference— Rules of construction and definitions, O.C.G.A. §§ 1-3-1—1-3-3.

Whenever in this Code or in any ordinance of the city any act is prohibited or is made or declared to be unlawful or an offense, or whenever in such Code or ordinance the doing of any act is required or the failure to do any act is declared to be unlawful, where no specific penalty is provided therefor, the violation of such provision of this Code or any such ordinance shall be punished by a fine not to exceed one thousand dollars ($1,000.00) or imprisonment in the city jail for not more than one hundred and eighty (180) days, or work in the workgang on the public streets or on such public works as the authorities may employ the workgang for not more than thirty (30) days, or by any one or more of these punishments, subject to all limitations contained in the Charter of the City. Each day any violation of this Code or of any ordinance shall continue shall constitute a separate offense.
However, unless otherwise specifically authorized by another city ordinance, the city judge, after prescribing a determinate jail sentence in days or months (if imprisonment is imposed), may not sentence a defendant to serve actual time in the city jail without first considering the extenuating and aggravating factors surrounding the case and the circumstances affecting the individual defendant. In fact, the city judge may suspend any and all jail time where a defendant is sentenced to imprisonment in the city jail if the imposition of such sentence, at the discretion of the judge, will not serve the interest of justice.
In exercising his or her discretion, when determining whether imprisonment of the defendant is in the best interest of justice, the city judge shall consider the extenuating and aggravating factors and circumstances surrounding the case and the individual defendant. Aggravating factors include, but are not limited to, the amount of damages caused by the defendant's actions to third parties, whether the defendant is a multiple offender, whether the defendant has prior criminal convictions, whether the defendant is employed, and such similar factors. Extenuating circumstances shall include, but are not limited to, whether the defendant is a first time offender, whether the defendant has repaired and/or repaid any damages caused as a result of his or her actions, whether the defendant is employed and has the ability to pay a fine, and such similar factors.
In addition to the penalties hereinabove provided, any condition caused or permitted to exist in violation of any of the provisions of this Code or any ordinance shall be deemed a public nuisance, and may be abated by the city as provided by law, and each day that such condition continues shall be regarded as a new and separate offense.
(Ord. No. 2005-23, § 1, 11-7-05; Ord. No. 2006-06, § 2, 2-6-06)

It is the finding of the mayor and council that it is in the best interest of justice that in those cases where a defendant or defendants enter a guilty plea or are found guilty of violating a city ordinance, that they be punished by the imposition of a fine rather than by imprisonment in the city jail. The mayor and council further find that the punishment of imprisonment should be used at the discretion of the judge in those cases in which, under the facts of the case and the circumstances surrounding the individual defendant, a fine may not be the appropriate punishment. The mayor and council further find that there should be guidelines for the judge to help him/her determine whether or not imprisonment is the appropriate punishment under the circumstances of the case after a defendant enters a guilty plea or is found guilty of violating a city ordinance.
Accordingly, the mayor and council find that it is in the best interest of the health, welfare, safety and morals of the community to provide guidelines for the imposition of the punishment of imprisonment in the city jail provided by section 1-8 of this Code of Ordinances. It is a matter of governmental interest and concern and in the interest of the public welfare to use the punishment of imprisonment in those cases in which the court, in its discretion and under the circumstances of the case, considers this punishment fitting in order to properly enforce the city ordinances. To that end, the ordinance from which this section derives is hereby adopted.
This ordinance is not intended as a de facto prohibition of the judge's discretion. This ordinance is intended to guide that discretion given to the judge by section 7-8 of the City Charter.
(Ord. No. 2006-06, § 2, 2-6-06)

(a) Authority; forfeiture; lien. The chief judge shall have authority to release any person arrested for a violation of any law, ordinance, regulation or rule of the municipal government upon such person giving bond payable to the city in an amount and surety to be approved by the chief judge, conditioned for the appearance of such person before the city court at the time and place specified in said bond and from time to time until such person shall have been discharged by the court. If any person so released under appearance bond shall fail to appear for trial at the time named therein, such bond shall be forfeited. However, the person released on appearance bond or the surety shall have thirty (30) days after forfeiture to show cause why such bond should not be forfeited. If no sufficient cause be shown, the forfeiture of said bond shall be final and absolute and execution shall issue for the full amount thereof, and all costs against the principal and sureties thereon. Such execution shall be signed by the city clerk and the city judge, and shall be directed to the chief of police and to all and singular the sheriffs of the state, and the same when so issued shall be a lien upon all property, real or personal of such parties, and of binding effect upon such parties, and the defendants therein as if the same were issued upon judgement in the superior courts, and shall be levied by any officers to whom it shall be directed.

(a) Purpose. The purpose of this section is to safeguard the protection of city assets and to provide guidelines and a procedure for the disposal of surplus property. This shall include all property purchased with city funds, grants, gifts, and donations to the city, or acquired through other means but ownership and title vest with the city.
(b) Definitions. The following words, terms, and phrases, when used in this section, shall have the meanings ascribed to them in this section:
(1) Excess supplies mean any supplies, other than expendable supplies, having a remaining useful life but which are no longer required by the using agency in possession of the supplies.
(2) Expendable supplies mean all tangible supplies other than nonexpendable supplies.
(3) Nonexpendable supplies mean all tangible supplies having an original acquisition cost of over one hundred dollars ($100.00) per unit and a probable useful life of more than one (1) year.
(4) Supplies means personal property, as distinguished from real property, consisting of all items, objects, devices, and tangible things used or useful to the city in carrying out its functions and operations. This includes, but is not limited to, vehicles, furniture, equipment, computers, electronic devices, firearms, uniforms, books, tools, and similar goods, whether expendable or durable in nature.
(5) Surplus supplies mean any supplies, other than expendable supplies, no longer having any use to the city. This includes obsolete supplies, scrap materials and nonexpendable supplies that have completed their useful life cycle.
(c) Duties of chief procurement officer. Under this section, the chief procurement officer ("CPO") shall be responsible for: (i) The sale, lease, donation, or disposal of surplus supplies by public auction, competitive sealed bidding, or other appropriate method in the best interests of the city, provided that no employee of the owning or disposing using agency shall be entitled to purchase such supplies; and (ii) the transfer of excess supplies to using agencies of the city.
(d) Policies and procedures.
(1) Consistent with this section, the CPO shall adopt operational procedures relating to supplies owned by the city during their entire life cycle.
(2) These procedures shall promote the objectives of city supply management, which include preventing waste, continuing utilization of supplies and obtaining a fair return of value upon disposal of supplies.
(3) The adopted procedures shall provide for inspection, testing, warehousing, inventory and effective transfer and disposition of supplies.
(4) No using agency shall transfer, sell, trade in or otherwise dispose of supplies owned by the city without written authorization of the chief procurement officer.
(5) No agency shall transfer, sell, trade or in any otherwise dispose of supplies to a member of city council or their immediate family members.
(e) Excess supplies. Under this section, using agencies shall notify the CPO, as necessary, of all excess supplies. The CPO shall transfer excess supplies to other city agencies as determined by need and in accordance with operational procedures adopted pursuant to this section.
(f) Disposition of surplus supplies.
(1) Generally. Unless otherwise provided in this section, the CPO shall dispose of any supplies owned by the city, upon the recommendation of and after consultation with the using agency, as provided in this section. Surplus supplies that have an estimated value more than two hundred dollars ($200.00) shall be offered through competitive sealed bids and public auction. Surplus supplies that have an estimated value of two hundred dollars ($200.00) or less may be offered by established markets, posted prices or by any other means advantageous to the city. The CPO shall determine the estimated value of the surplus property to be sold. Notwithstanding this paragraph, the CPO may exchange or trade in surplus supplies with another property owner if such exchange or trade is deemed to be in the best interests of the city.
(2) Competitive sealed bidding.
a. Solicitation and opening. When making sales of surplus supplies by competitive sealed bidding, notice of the sale shall be given by advertisement in a newspaper of general circulation at least once no less than fifteen (15) nor more than sixty (60) days before the date set for receipt of bids. Notice may also be given by mailing an invitation for sale bids to prospective offerors, including those offerors on lists maintained for this purpose, and by making invitation for sale bids publicly available. The invitation for sale bids shall list supplies offered for sale, designate their location and how they may be inspected, and state the terms and conditions of sale and instructions to offerors, including the place, date, and time for bid opening. Bids shall be opened publicly.
b. Award. The award shall be made in accordance with the provisions of the invitation for sale bids to the highest responsible offeror, provided that the price offered by such offeror is acceptable to the CPO. If such price is not acceptable, the CPO may reject the bids in whole or in part and negotiate the sale, provided the negotiated sale price is higher than the highest responsive and responsible offeror's price, or the CPO may resolicit bids.
c. Auctions. Supplies may be sold at public auction. Notice of such auction shall be given by advertisement in a newspaper of general circulation at least once, no less than fifteen (15) nor more than sixty (60) days before the day of the auction. When appropriate, an experienced auctioneer should cry the sale and assist in preparation of sale. The notice shall contain a general description of the property to be sold, all the terms and conditions of the sale, that a deposit may be required to participate in the bidding, that the purchaser must remove within a stated time all surplus supplies purchased and that the city retains the right to reject any and all bids.
(3) Established markets, posted prices, and trade-in. Surplus supplies which have an estimated value of five hundred dollars ($500.00) or less may be sold in established markets where such supplies, including but not limited to livestock and produce, are regularly sold in wholesale lots and prices are set by open competition. Surplus supplies may be sold at posted prices as determined by the CPO, provided that such prices are based on fair market value and the sale is conducted pursuant to procedures established under this section. Surplus supplies may be traded in only when the CPO determines that the trade-in value is expected to exceed the value estimated to be obtained through the sale or other disposition of such supplies.
(4) Disposal by internal transfer. Priority is given to city departments to repurpose surplus items. The only cost to a department for an internal transfer of goods is the costs of moving and installing the item(s). Assets will be posted a minimum of five (5) business days. In situations where there is a competing department interest, the property will be redeployed based on a best identified use by the CPO on a first come, first served basis.
(5) Disposal by donation. Items that cannot be used or sold may be donated "as is" to an approved not-for-profit institution upon written approval from the appropriate department and the CPO. The CPO shall issue a surplus property bill of sale for all items the city donates to a not-for-profit.
(6) Disposed items. Items that cannot be sold or donated will be discarded through the city's normal waste removal process. Disposal requests must be approved by the department and division heads.
(7) Payment for surplus supplies. Only U.S. postal money orders, certified checks, and cashier's checks shall be accepted for sales of surplus property; except cash or a personal check may be accepted for petty cash sales of less than one hundred dollars ($100.00). A copy of all sales notices or invoices shall be sent to the chief financial officer.
(g) Disposition of proceeds of sale, lease, donation, or disposal. Upon completion of sale, lease, donation, or disposal of surplus or excess property owned by the city as provided in this section, the CPO shall notify the chief financial officer in writing, which notice shall contain as a minimum, a description of the property sold, the inventory control number, the amount for which the article was sold and the using agency in which the property was used. The chief financial officer shall make the necessary corrections to the inventory of the city. The CPO shall pay the proceeds of such sale, lease or disposal of property owned by the city to the chief financial officer, as required by law.

(a) Scope. The mayor and city council shall conduct all meetings in accordance with state law, the Charter, and the parliamentary procedures set forth herein. The mayor and council hereby affirm and adopt Robert's Rules of Order as the parliamentary rules to govern the conduct of meetings to the extent any matter, procedure, or order is not otherwise covered in this Code Section.
(b) Call to order. The mayor shall call all meetings to order at the appointed time. In accordance with section 1-8 of the Charter, the mayor shall preside over the deliberations of city council to assure full participation in accordance with these rules.
(c) Order of consideration. Except as otherwise provided in these rules or determined by mayor and council, the items listed on the meeting agenda shall be considered in numerical order, and the city clerk shall be responsible for sounding the items listed on the meeting agenda.
(d) Mayor's neutrality. In order to ensure his or her neutrality, while presiding over the deliberations of city council in accordance with the Charter, the mayor shall not express opinions or otherwise participate in the debate on matters before city council.
(e) Limit on remarks. Each council member shall limit his or her remarks to a reasonable duration.
(f) Recognition of speakers. At all meetings, it shall be the responsibility of the city manager to recognize city council members wishing to speak on agenda items and to tally the votes cast, but the city manager shall carry out these functions through the use of a suitable electronic system approved by mayor and council.
(g) Citizen remarks. Mayor and council may extend the time for an individual citizen to speak during the public comment portion of any meeting and may also extend the total time allotted for public comments at any meeting.
(h) Mayor and council closing remarks. The mayor and each member of city council shall be entitled to make closing remarks at the conclusion of each meeting; however, the mayor shall at all times be first in the order of speakers.
(i) City attorney as parliamentarian.
(1) Appointment and role of parliamentarian. The city attorney shall serve as the official parliamentarian for all meetings of the mayor and city council. In such capacity, the city attorney shall advise the mayor, city council, and city staff regarding parliamentary procedure, compliance with the Charter, this Code, or other applicable law.
(2) Authority to raise procedural concerns. During any meeting of the mayor and city council, the city attorney, in the capacity as parliamentarian, may independently raise a point of order, parliamentary inquiry, procedural clarification, or legal concern whenever the city attorney determines that clarification or intervention is necessary to ensure compliance with applicable law, the Charter, this Code, adopted procedures, or Robert's Rules of Order. The city attorney may also provide such procedural or legal guidance upon the request of the mayor or any member of the city council.
(3) Authority to admonish and maintain order. The city attorney shall also admonish the mayor and city council when there is a breach of decorum and good order in a meeting, when debate has strayed from the subject at hand, or when debate has grown redundant or so excessive in duration that it is rendered ineffective. In such instances, the city attorney shall actively speak up and intervene to maintain the orderly and efficient operation of the meeting, recommending such motions or measures as are deemed appropriate.
(4) Recognition for parliamentary guidance. The mayor, as presiding officer, shall recognize the city attorney for the limited purpose of providing parliamentary or legal guidance when requested by a member of the governing body or when the city attorney determines intervention is necessary pursuant to this subsection. Nothing herein shall be construed to authorize the city attorney to vote, deliberate policy matters, or otherwise participate as a member of the governing body. Further, nothing herein shall be construed to abrogate the role of the mayor as presiding officer under the charter.
(5) Purpose and construction. The provisions of this subsection are intended to promote the orderly conduct of meetings, ensure consistent application of parliamentary procedure, and protect compliance with applicable law. Parliamentary guidance provided by the city attorney shall be advisory in nature and shall not supersede any lawful action of the mayor and city council.
(6) Repeated procedural violations by presiding officer. In the event the presiding officer has been advised by the city attorney acting as parliamentarian on three (3) or more occasions during the same meeting regarding a breach of decorum and good order or noncompliance with applicable parliamentary procedures, the Charter, or this Code, any member of city council may move to designate the mayor pro tem as presiding officer for the remainder of that meeting. Such motion shall require the unanimous affirmative vote of the council members present and voting. Upon approval of such motion, the mayor pro tem shall preside over the remainder of the meeting with the same procedural authority as the mayor for purposes of conducting the meeting and maintaining order. The mayor shall not be removed from office or from attendance at the meeting by virtue of such action and shall retain any voting authority expressly provided by the Charter, including the authority to vote in the event of a tie. Upon assuming the role of presiding officer pursuant to this subsection, the mayor pro tem shall exercise the duties of the chair in a neutral capacity and shall not deliberate on matters before the governing body during the remainder of the meeting but shall retain all voting rights otherwise afforded as a member of city council under the Charter and applicable law.
(7) Repeated procedural violations by council member. In the event a member of city council has been advised by the city attorney acting as parliamentarian on three (3) or more occasions during the same meeting regarding a breach of decorum and good order or noncompliance with applicable parliamentary procedures, the Charter, this Code, or lawful rulings of the presiding officer, any member of city council may move to limit the offending member's privilege to further deliberate or discuss agenda items for the remainder of the meeting. Such motion shall require the unanimous affirmative vote of the remaining council members present and voting, excluding the member who is the subject of the motion. Upon approval of such motion, the affected council member shall remain entitled to attend the meeting and cast votes on all matters properly before the governing body but shall not be recognized for further deliberation, debate, or discussion during the remainder of the meeting except as necessary to make legally required disclosures relating to conflicts of interest or abstentions.

As used in this article, the following terms shall have the following meanings, unless the context clearly indicates that a different meaning is intended:
Censure means the act of condemning as wrong. A censure shall be effectuated by entry in the minutes of a city council meeting.
City official and/or official, unless otherwise expressly defined, means the mayor, members of the city council, candidates for the offices of the mayor and city council after legal notice of candidacy and qualification as such candidate, municipal court judges (including substitute judges), and individuals appointed by the mayor and council to all city commissions, authorities, committees, boards and task forces, and all other city committee and/or body members, unless specifically exempted from this article by law and/or the city council.
Complainant means a person or entity who submits to the city clerk an ethics complaint alleging violations of this article.
Decision means any article, resolution, contract, franchise, formal action or other matter voted on by the city council or other city board or commission, as well as the discussions or deliberations, of the council, board or commission which can or may lead to a vote or formal action by such body.
Discretionary authority means the power to exercise any judgment in a decision or action.
Ethics complaint means a written document alleging a violation of this article by a city official, any employee, or appointee. All ethics complaints filed with the city shall contain the following:
(1) A brief statement specifically identifying the name and title of the city official, employee, or appointee against whom the complaint is filed. An ethics complaint may not allege violations and/or seek action against more than one city official, employee, or appointee;
(2) A numbered list separately identifying each improper act which the city official, employee, or appointee is alleged to have committed, including: 1) the date of any such alleged offense(s), 2) the specific section(s) of this article that each act is alleged to be in violation of; and 3) the factual basis for each alleged violation;
(3) A sworn and notarized statement by the complainant attesting that all information in the ethics complaint is true to the complainant's information and knowledge;
(4) Email address, phone number and mailing address where the complainant may be contacted; and
(5) The complainant's residential address within the city limits.
Entity means a sole proprietorship, partnership, limited partnership, firm, corporation, professional corporation, holding company, joint stock company, receivership, trust or any other entity recognized by law through which business may be conducted.
Exempt city boards, commissions, authorities, and similar bodies shall mean all boards, commissions, authorities, and similar bodies of the city other than the planning commission, board of zoning appeals, design review commission, and any authority created by either the Georgia General Assembly or by the city pursuant to O.C.G.A. Tit. 36, Chs. 61 and 62. The members of exempt city boards, commissions, authorities, and similar bodies are specifically exempted from the requirements of this article unless such member is either an elected official of the city or is also a member of another city board, commission, authority or similar body not specifically exempted by this article or by law.
Financial gain means any interest which shall yield, directly or indirectly, a monetary or other material benefit to another person, entity, or business, other than the duly authorized salary or compensation for that person, entity, or business for its services to the city.
Financial interest means any interest which shall yield, directly or indirectly, a monetary or other material benefit to the official or employee, other than the duly authorized salary or compensation for the official's or employee's services to the city, or to any person employing or retaining the services of the official or employee or to the official's or employee's immediate family.
Immediate family means the legal and/or biological parent, sibling, child, spouse, or any corresponding in-law, of any city official, employee, or appointee.
Interest:
(1) Incidental interest means an interest in a person, entity or property which is not a substantial interest.
(2) Remote interest means an interest of a person or entity, including a city official, who would be affected in the same way as the general public. The interest of a council member in the property tax rate, general city fees, city utility charges, or a comprehensive zoning article or similar decisions is incidental to the extent that the council member would be affected in common with the general public.
(3) Substantial interest means a known interest, either directly or through a member of the immediate family, in another person or entity:
a. The interest is ownership of five (5) percent or more of the voting stock, shares or equity of an entity, excluding investments held inside mutual funds or managed accounts;
b. The interest is ownership of five thousand dollars ($5,000.00) or more of the equity or market value of the entity, excluding (i) entities with a market capitalization of five hundred million dollars ($500,000,000.00) or more, and (ii) investments held inside mutual funds or managed accounts;
c. Funds received by the person from the other person or entity either during the previous twelve (12) months equaled or exceeded five thousand dollars ($5,000.00) in salary, bonuses, commissions or professional fees, or ten (10) percent of the recipient's gross income during that period, whichever is less;
d. The person serves as a corporate officer or member of the board of directors or other governing board of the for-profit entity other than a corporate entity owned or created by the city council;
e. The person is a creditor, debtor or guarantor of the other person or entity in an amount of five thousand dollars ($5,000.00) or more; or
f. An equitable or legal ownership interest in real property with a market value of five thousand dollars ($5,000.00) or more.
Reprimand means an official reproof, reprehension, or rebuke of a wrong. A reprimand shall be effectuated by resolution of the mayor and council.
Respondent means a city official, employee, or appointee charged with a violation of this article.

(1) This prohibition shall not be applicable to the professional activities of the city attorney in his or her work as an independent contractor and legal advisor on behalf of the city.

(a) Name and commencement. There is hereby created a body known as the board of ethics for the City of College Park, Georgia ("board of ethics"), which shall commence on July 1, 2025.
(b) Powers and duties. The board of ethics shall have the following powers and duties:

(c) Board composition. The board of ethics shall be composed of a total of five (5) directors. No director shall reside within the City of College Park, Georgia. Additionally, three (3) of the directors must be attorneys actively licensed within the State of Georgia.

The city manager and the city attorney shall provide a list of all applicable candidates to the city council for consideration and approval.
(e) Board term. Directors shall serve staggered terms in accordance with this section. (a) Preliminary review of ethics complaints.
(1) Upon being appointed and being served with all pertinent documents, and upon expiration of the 15-day period for the respondent to file an answer, the board of ethics shall review the complaint and response, if any, to determine: (i) whether the complaint is in conformity with the requirements of sections 2-75 and 2-82 herein, (ii) whether upon consideration of the complaint and response, the complaint is unjustified, frivolous, patently unfounded, or (iii) whether upon consideration of the complaint and answer, the complaint demonstrates facts sufficient to invoke disciplinary jurisdiction as set forth in this article.
(2) If the complaint fails to meet the requirements of subsection (1) above or any other procedural requirement in this Code, the complaining party shall be afforded a period of time not to exceed five (5) business days to cure such failure. A dismissal of such complaint preliminarily herein shall not deprive the complaining party of any action such party might otherwise have at law or in equity. A complaint shall be dismissed only on the following grounds:
(i) The complaint was filed against a person not covered by section 2-74;
(ii) The complaining party does not meet the residency requirement set forth on section 2-82(a);
(iii) The complaint is unjustified, frivolous, or patently unfounded, as described in section 2-84(a)(1)(ii);
(iv) The facts alleged in the complaint do not invoke the disciplinary jurisdiction of this Code under section 2-84(a)(1)(iii);
(v) The complaint is barred by section 2-85; or
(vi) The complaint is outside the statute of limitations in section 2-87.
(b) Evidentiary hearing on ethics complaints.
(1) Upon a determination that the complaint should not be dismissed pursuant to subsection (a)(2) above, the board of ethics shall be empowered to collect evidence and information concerning such complaint and to add the findings and results of the investigation to the file containing such complaint.
(i) The board of ethics may seek such further information from the complainant or the respondent through inquiry or written questions, provided, however, the respondent shall have no obligation to answer any inquiries; or
(ii) The board of ethics shall conduct a hearing regarding the allegations set forth in the complaint. Respondent shall have the right to representation by counsel at all stages of these proceedings, to written notice of the hearing at least ten (10) calendar days before the first hearing, to hear and examine the evidence and witnesses, to not testify, and to submit evidence and call or subpoena witnesses to oppose or mitigate the allegations. In all hearings held under this section, the procedures and rules of evidence applicable in civil cases shall guide, but not strictly apply.
(2) All investigations under this section shall be completed within forty-five (45) days of the board of ethics receiving the complaint and any response. Should the investigation not be completed in the said period, the complaint will be deemed dismissed as a failure to state facts sufficient to invoke the disciplinary jurisdiction of the city council, unless an extension is requested by complainant and granted by the board of ethics. Only one such extension may be granted for an additional thirty (30) days.
(i) Within seven (7) days of the completion of the investigation, the board of ethics shall either:
1. Dismiss the complaint on the grounds that it is unjustified, frivolous, patently unfounded, or that it fails to state facts sufficient to invoke the disciplinary jurisdiction of the city council; or
2. Prepare a report of findings and recommendations to the mayor and city council.
(ii) Should the board of ethics determine to submit a report in the matter, the report shall consist of: A written finding of facts, a determination whether the complaint establishes beyond a reasonable doubt that a violation has been committed, and, if so, the specific violation and evidence supporting the same, and a recommendation regarding the punishment for such violation.
(iii) The board of ethics' written determination of findings and recommendations shall be delivered to the city clerk, who shall provide a copy to the city manager and the mayor and council and serve a copy on the complainant and respondent by personal service, certified mail return receipt requested, or by statutory overnight delivery. Such findings shall not be final until approved by vote of the city council.
(c) Mayor and city council.
(1) Upon receipt of findings and recommendations from the the board of ethics, the mayor and council may:
(i) By simple majority accept the findings of the board of ethics.
(ii) By simple majority accept the findings of fact and reject the recommended discipline, instead substituting its own discipline which shall be limited to the remedies stated herein.
(iii) By a supermajority, consisting of the majority of those present forming a quorum plus one, reject the findings and recommendations and conduct its own hearing in conjunction with the same hearing procedures dictated above. Upon the completion of such a hearing, the findings and recommendations of the mayor and city council shall be binding.
(iv) If no majority or supermajority can be obtained as provided herein, the findings and recommendations shall be deemed rejected and the complaint dismissed. Such dismissal shall be one on the merits.
(2) If the subject of the complaint is the mayor or any council member, he or she shall recuse themselves from participation in any hearing or vote held pursuant to this subsection (c), with the exception of the right to attend such hearing as member of the general public, nor shall such mayor or council member be counted for the purpose of establishing a quorum.
(3) Upon final judgment and certification of the minutes of the meeting disposing of this matter, the city clerk shall serve the respondent with the copy of the certified minutes and findings and recommendations by personal service, certified mail return receipt requested or statutory overnight service.

(a) Chief city court judge. The mayor and council may appoint an individual to serve as chief judge to preside over the city's municipal court. The chief judge shall be responsible for the general supervision of the city court and shall promulgate all rules necessary for the supervision, conduct, and administration of the court.
(b) City court judge pro tem. The mayor and council may appoint a city court judge pro tem, who shall be acting city court judge in the absence, disability or disqualification of the chief judge. The acting city court judge shall have all the powers and perform all the duties of the chief municipal court judge when necessary.
(c) In-person proceedings. Except as otherwise required by state law, judicial emergency order, or specific authorization by the Georgia Judicial Council, all proceedings of the City Court of College Park shall be conducted in person at such times and locations as designated by the chief city court judge. The chief judge shall ensure that in-person sessions of court are held on a regular schedule and in a manner accessible to the public, consistent with applicable legal and procedural requirements. Remote or virtual court proceedings may be authorized only upon a finding that such format is necessary to serve the interests of justice, ensure public safety, or comply with a directive from a state judicial authority. This provision shall not be construed to prohibit the use of electronic or remote technology for administrative coordination, pretrial communications, or non-judicial functions, as permitted by law.
(d) Regular court sessions. Court must be held in session at regular intervals as determined by the chief city court judge, and in no case shall the court be inactive for unreasonable periods without cause.
(e) Appointment and authority of solicitors.
(1) The mayor and council shall have the authority to appoint one (1) or more individuals to serve as solicitor(s) of the city court. Solicitors so appointed shall be authorized to prosecute violations of city ordinances and such other matters as may be within the jurisdiction of the city court, including, but not limited to, traffic offenses, code enforcement matters, and environmental violations. The mayor and council shall assign one (1) or more solicitors to each administrative division of the city court, including the court services division and the environmental division referred to in section 2-106. These solicitors shall be responsible for the prosecution of all matters within their assigned division and shall coordinate with relevant city departments and court staff to ensure the effective administration of justice.
(2) The office of solicitor may, at the discretion of the mayor and council, be held concurrently by the city attorney, provided that any prosecutorial duties undertaken by the city attorney in such capacity do not conflict with their responsibilities as legal counsel to the city. In the event of a conflict or potential conflict, the mayor and council may appoint an alternate or additional solicitor to handle such matters independently.
(3) All solicitors shall serve at the pleasure of the mayor and council and may be appointed for such term and under such conditions as the governing body deems appropriate, including but not limited to engagement by contract, agreement, or resolution.
(4) Solicitors shall coordinate with the chief judge, court administration, law enforcement, code enforcement, and other relevant city departments to facilitate the orderly and effective prosecution of matters before the city court. Nothing in this subsection shall be construed to grant enforcement or investigative authority to the solicitor outside the scope of lawful prosecution.
(5) All solicitors shall be members in good standing of the State Bar of Georgia and shall meet such other qualifications as may be prescribed by law or ordinance.
(Ord. No. 2025-23, § 1(Exh. A), 11-3-25)
205:
(a) Purpose. The purpose of this section is to formally establish internal administrative divisions within the City Court of College Park for the purpose of improving case flow management, facilitating coordination with municipal departments, and ensuring the efficient and effective handling of matters within the jurisdiction of the court.
(b) Establishment of divisions. The City Court of College Park shall consist of the following two (2) administrative divisions. These divisions shall be internal administrative designations and shall not confer separate jurisdiction or alter the authority of the city court as established by law.
(1) Court services division. The court services division, also referred to as "traffic court," shall be responsible for the adjudication of cases involving traffic offenses, motor vehicle violations, and related ordinance infractions occurring within the City of College Park. This division shall operate in accordance with applicable provisions of state law, city ordinances, and court procedures.
(2) Environmental division. The environmental division, also referred to as "environmental court," shall be responsible for the adjudication of cases involving violations of the city's environmental, sanitation, property maintenance, code enforcement, and blight remediation ordinances. The environmental division shall coordinate with the city's code enforcement and public works departments for scheduling, documentation, and enforcement support related to such cases.
(c) Judicial assignments to divisions. The chief city court judge may preside over matters assigned to the court services division. The city court judge pro tem, as appointed by the mayor and council pursuant to this Code, may be administratively assigned to preside over matters in the environmental division. This assignment shall be for the purpose of efficient case management and does not constitute the creation of a new court or judicial office. All judges shall exercise authority solely within the jurisdiction of the City Court of College Park as established by the city charter and applicable state law.
(d) Internal operations. Each division shall operate within the framework of the city court and shall utilize existing court staff, scheduling procedures, and case management systems. The establishment of divisions shall not require separate funding, judicial appointments, or facilities unless authorized by ordinance or budget appropriation.
(e) Coordination with city departments. To ensure administrative efficiency, the environmental division shall maintain regular coordination with the city's code enforcement, public works, and other relevant departments. This coordination shall be administrative in nature and shall not confer enforcement or prosecutorial powers upon court personnel.
(f) Oversight and reporting. The city manager or their designee may request periodic administrative reports regarding the caseloads and scheduling practices of each division for the purpose of coordination with municipal departments and resource planning. Such oversight shall not interfere with the judicial independence or decision-making authority of the judges of the city court.
(g) No expansion of jurisdiction. Nothing in this section shall be construed to expand, limit, or otherwise modify the subject matter or territorial jurisdiction of the City Court of College Park as established by the city charter or applicable state law.
(Ord. No. 2025-23, § 1(Exh. A), 11-3-25)

The purpose of this chapter is to regulate the installation and use of police and fire alarm systems and to establish standards for, controls of, and maintenance of the various alarm systems that are intended to bring about police and/or fire department response.
(Ord. No. 86-33, § 1, 12-8-86)
216:
(a) Alarm system shall mean an assembly of equipment and devices designated and arranged to detect and signal an unauthorized intrusion into a premise, to signal an attempted robbery at protected premises, a fire on premises, a medical emergency needing medical attention, and/or an ambulance, or like occurrences.
(b) False alarm shall mean the activation of an alarm system where none of the emergencies for which the alarm system has been installed have, in fact, occurred.
(c) Response shall mean the dispatch of police, fire equipment, ambulance, or other appropriate equipment for the emergency signal, to the premises where the alarm system has been activated indicating such emergency is present.
(d) Licensing authority means the City of College Park, Georgia, through the police and fire chief of said city.
(e) Police and fire chief means the chief of police of the College Park Police Department, and the fire chief of the College Park Fire Department, all of College Park, Georgia and/or their authorized representatives.
(Ord. No. 86-33, § 2, 12-8-86)
217:
(a) Application for permits. Any property owner or lessee of property in the City of College Park having or installing on his or its premises an alarm system shall apply to the licensing authority on a form to be supplied by the licensing authority for a permit to have such a device on his or its premises. Application for permits for alarm systems existing on premises on the effective date of this article must be made to the licensing authority within ninety (90) days of the effective date of this chapter. No such alarm system may be installed on the premises of the owner or lessee after the effective date of this chapter prior to the licensing authority having issued a permit to such owner or lessee. No presently existing alarm system shall be modified after the effective date of this chapter prior to the issuance of a permit to such owner or lessee by the licensing authority.
(b) Permit fees. The annual permit fee for an alarm system shall be ten dollars ($10.00) per year for a system that is not directly monitored by the College Park Police and Fire Departments. The annual permit fee for an alarm system directly monitored by the College Park Police and Fire Departments shall be fifty dollars ($50.00).
(c) Suspension or revocation; false alarms. A permit issued under this article may be suspended or revoked by the licensing authority for any violation of this chapter or for an excess of four (4) nonvalid alarms to which the police department or fire department responds within a calendar year. No part of the permit fee shall be refunded when a permit is suspended or revoked. No permit issued under this article shall be suspended or revoked prior to a hearing to be held by the licensing authority after giving five (5) days written notice to the owner or lessee. In addition hereto, any permit holder who shall have in excess of three (3) false alarms within a calendar year shall be guilty of a violation of this chapter and punishable by a fine of twenty-five dollars ($25.00) per each false alarm during such calendar year in excess of the first three (3) false alarms. Notwithstanding anything contained in this paragraph (c) to the contrary, a permittee installing or having installed on his premises a new alarm system shall be granted a grace period of thirty (30) days beginning with the date of the new installation during which grace period the provisions hereof concerning the suspension or revocation of the permit or the imposition of a fine shall not apply.
(d) Appeal. Any owner or lessee whose permit has been denied, or whose permit has been suspended or revoked, may appeal such denial, suspension or revocation in writing to the mayor and council within thirty (30) days after the date of the notice of the denial, suspension or revocation and may appear before the mayor and council at a time and place to be determined by the mayor and council in support of his or its contention that the permit should not have been denied, suspended, or revoked. In all cases, the decision of the mayor and council is final.
(e) Force majeure. In determining the number of nonvalid alarms, the licensing authority may exclude any nonvalid alarm which it determines was caused by an act of God, power failure and/or telephone line interruption.
(f) Renewal. All holders of alarm system permits must tender an annual permit fee to the licensing authority on or before January 1 of each year. Failure to pay such permit fee in the time and manner provided will result in the suspension or revocation of the permit.
(g) Connection. A holder of an alarm system permit may not connect its alarm system to in any way directly notify the police department or fire department without first obtaining an alarm system permit. All costs incurred in such hookup shall be borne by the permittee. No alarm business or permit holder shall place, install, or otherwise locate any central station equipment for direct connection of alarm systems in the police department or fire department without its prior consent. Upon suspension or revocation of such permit, the owner or lessee shall immediately disconnect his or its alarm system.
(h) Alarm system description. The alarm agent and/or alarm business must provide the owner or lessee of the alarm system a written description of the function and operation of the alarm system installed on the premises, along with the procedure and means for activating or deactivating the same.
(i) Individual requirement. Every person maintaining an alarm system shall furnish to the police chief and fire chief the name and telephone number of the primary individual responsible for the alarm system and at least one alternate name and telephone number of an individual who can deactivate the alarm system or systems. The owner or lessee of an alarm system will be responsible for deactivating the alarm system within a reasonable time following notification by the police department or fire department.
(Ord. No. 86-33, § 3, 12-8-86)

As used in this chapter, the following terms shall have the respective meanings ascribed to them:
(1) Alcohol means ethyl alcohol, hydrated oxide of ethyl, or spirits of wine, from whatever source or by whatever process produced.
(2) Alcoholic beverage means and includes all alcohol, distilled spirits, beer, malt beverage, wine, or fortified wine.
(3) Ancillary retailer means a for-profit commercial business or non-profit organization located within the city, including but not limited to a cigar bar, dog park, art gallery, museum, or theater, located within the Downtown Commercial District, Hospitality Campus District, Transit Oriented Development District, or Planned Development District that is licensed under this chapter to sell alcoholic beverages for consumption on its premises. Ancillary commercial retailer shall not mean any business that derives more than twenty (20) percent of its total annual gross revenues from the sale of alcoholic beverages.
(4) Brewer means a manufacturer of malt beverages.
(5) Brewpub means any eating establishment, as defined herein, in which malt beverages are manufactured, subject to the barrel limitation in O.C.G.A. § 3-5-36.
(6) Complimentary service means the gratis provision of malt beverages or wine served in connection with a service provided by a business, such as a salon, barbershop, or spa, to patrons for consumption on the premises pursuant to a complimentary service license issued under this chapter.
(7) Craft beer means a malt beverage produced at a brewery whose annual production is six million (6,000,000) barrels of beer or less (approximately three (3) percent of U.S. annual sales). Craft beer production is attributed to the rules of alternating proprietorships and the total beverage alcohol volume and flavor is derived from traditional or innovative brewing ingredients and their fermentation.
(8) Craft beer and wine market means a retail establishment which derives at least seventy (70) percent of its total annual gross sales from the sale of craft beers, hard cider, and/or wine.
(9) Distilled spirits means any alcoholic beverage obtained by distillation or containing more than twenty-four (24) percent alcohol by volume, including, but not limited to, all fortified wines.
(10) Distiller means a manufacturer of distilled spirits.
(11) Eating establishment means an establishment open to the public, with no cover charge or fee for entry, which is licensed to sell distilled spirits, malt beverages, and/or wines for consumption on the premises and which derives at least fifty (50) percent of its total annual gross food and beverage sales from the sale of prepared meals or food as its principal business purpose. In order to be licensed for consumption of alcoholic beverages on the premises under this chapter, eating establishments are expected to keep and maintain regular days and hours of operation, at least four (4) days per week, as a convenience to the public, other than holidays, vacations, and periods when closed for repairs or remodeling. When determining the total annual gross food and beverage sales for eating establishments operating as a brewpub, barrels of malt beverages sold to licensed wholesale dealers, or packaged in bottles or growlers sold to the public for consumption off the premises, shall not be used. An eating establishment shall not mean a business that requires a cover charge or fee to gain entry into the premises; provided, however, eating establishments may hold a maximum of six (6) ticketed events, as defined herein, annually.
(12) Family includes any person related to the holder of a license within the first degree of consanguinity or affinity as computed according to civil law.
(13) Farm winery means a winery which makes at least forty (40) percent of its annual production from agricultural produce grown in the state where the winery is located and:
a. Is located on premises, a substantial portion of which is used for agricultural purposes, including the cultivation of grapes, berries, or fruits to be utilized in the manufacture or production of wine by the winery; or
b. Is owned and operated by persons who are engaged in the production of a substantial portion of the agricultural produce used in its annual production.
c. To the extent that the definition of "farm winery" in this subsection differs from the definition provided in O.C.G.A. § 3-6-21.1, the definition in O.C.G.A. § 3-6-21.1 controls.
(14) Farm winery tasting room means an outlet for the promotion of a farm winery's wine by providing samples of such wine to the public and for the sale of such wine at retail for consumption on the premises and for sale in closed packages for consumption off the premises. Samples of wine can be given free of charge or for a fee. To the extent that the definition of "farm winery tasting room" in this subsection differs from the definition provided in O.C.G.A. § 3-6-21.1, the definition in O.C.G.A. § 3-6-21.1 controls.
(15) Food means all edible substances appropriate for human consumption as determined by the health department inspecting the city's eating establishments, which is sold or provided to the public by a licensee. Food shall not be construed to mean: olives, cherries, limes, lemons, salt, pepper, pineapples, celery, tomato juice, or any other fruit, vegetable or dairy product such as ice cream, cream, yogurt, milk or soft drinks, water, tonic water, other non-alcoholic carbonated or non-carbonated beverages when such items are used in alcoholic beverages or mixed drinks as an essential part of the beverage, mixed drink, or as a garnish thereon.
(16) Growler means a bottle, container or vessel, with a capacity not exceeding sixty-four (64) ounces that is designed for and especially intended to be filled with a craft beer or hard cider from a keg by a licensee or employee of a licensed brewpub or craft beer and wine market for off-premises consumption pursuant to this chapter. A refilled growler that has been properly sealed shall be considered an "unbroken package" for purposes of this chapter.
(17) Hard cider means an alcoholic beverage obtained by the fermentation of the juice of fruit, including, but not limited to, flavored or carbonated cider. For the purposes of this chapter, hard cider shall be deemed a malt beverage; provided, that it shall not contain more than seven (7) percent alcohol by volume.
(18) Hotel means every building or other structure kept, used, maintained, advertised and held out to the public to be a place where food is actually served and consumed and sleeping accommodations are offered for adequate pay to travelers and guests, whether transient, permanent or residential. To meet the definition of "hotel" under this chapter the facility must have fifty (50) or more rooms used for sleeping accommodations of such guests and one (1) or more public dining rooms, with an adequate and sanitary kitchen and a seating capacity of at least sixty (60) persons, where meals are regularly served to such guests. All sleeping accommodations and dining rooms must be conducted in the same building or in separate buildings or structures used in connection therewith that are on the same premises and are a part of the hotel operation. Motels meeting the qualifications set out herein for hotels shall be classified in the same category as hotels. Hotels shall have the privilege of granting franchises for the operation of a lounge or eating establishment in their premises, and the holder of such franchise shall be eligible for a license under the "hotel" classification.

Provided, however, a stockholder shall not be deemed to have an interest in an alcoholic beverage establishment where such stockholder owns stock in a motel or hotel having two hundred (200) or more rooms with an alcoholic beverage establishment located on the premises of such motel or hotel and owned by such motel or hotel. a. The operator of the business, if that business is operated by an individual; or
b. A partner of the partnership that operates the business, or an officer duly appointed by said partnership; or
c. An officer of the corporation which operates the business; or
d. Any individual named as a license representative of the business in accordance with this chapter.

b. In the case of malt beverages, any brewer; and

(27) Microdistillery means an establishment in which not more than 10,000 barrels of distilled spirits are manufactured on the licensed premises in a calendar year and in which such manufactured distilled spirits may be sold for consumption on the premises and consumption off premises, subject to the limitations prescribed in O.C.G.A. § 3-4-24.2. As used in this definition, the term "barrel" shall be defined as set forth in O.C.G.A. § 3-4-1.

a. For a premises regarding which no such license was issued the prior year; or
b. By a person or entity to whom no license was issued the prior year for the premises that is the subject of the license application.

(34) Private residence means a house, dwelling or structure wherein not less than one (1), nor more than two (2) families reside and shall not include a mobile home court, an apartment house having facilities for housing more than two (2) families, nor a boarding or rooming house where there are five (5) or more boarders or roomers. a. Primarily engaged in the retail sale of distilled spirits, malt beverages, and wine in unbroken packages, not for consumption on the premises, except as otherwise authorized herein; and
b. Which derives from such retail sale of alcoholic beverages in unbroken packages at least seventy-five (75) percent of its total annual gross sales from the sale of a combination of distilled spirits, malt beverages, and wine.

(40) Wine means any alcoholic beverage containing not more than twenty-four (24) percent alcohol by volume made from fruits, berries, or grapes either by natural fermentation or by natural fermentation with brandy added. The term includes, but is not limited to, all sparkling wines, champagnes, combinations of such beverages, vermouths, special natural wines, rectified wines, and like products. The term does not include cooking wine mixed with salt or other ingredients so as to render it unfit for human consumption as a beverage. (a) No license shall be granted under this chapter to any applicant: (i) Who is not a citizen or resident legal alien of the United States, (ii) who does not permanently reside in the Metropolitan Atlanta area, (iii) who refuses to complete and pass a background check as required by the city, or (iv) who currently owes the city any past-due debt (of any kind whatsoever), any tax (current or past-due), any fee, any fine, any monetary penalty or any other moneys otherwise due to the city.

The license representative must be twenty-one (21) years of age and a manager at the business location for which the applicant is seeking a license to serve alcohol. In the case of corporate applicants whose primary business is the operation of an alcoholic beverage store, the majority stockholder must meet the requirements of individual applicants under this subsection at the time application is made and at all times during which the license is in effect. If the applicant is a partner in a partnership, the requirements of this section shall apply to all partners at the time of application, and at all times during which the license is in effect.
(d) All applicants for licenses, whether for original or renewal, must attach to their applications evidence of their good character. No license, whether original or renewal, shall be issued to any person, partnership or corporation organized for pecuniary gain, or to the license representative of any such person, partnership or corporation, if any individual having an interest either as owner, partner, stockholder, manager, or operator, directly or indirectly, beneficial or absolute, or such person's spouse shall have been convicted of or shall have taken a plea of guilty or nolo contendere to:
(1) Within the five (5) years immediately prior to filing:
a. Any felony.
b. Any violation of any law regulating gambling, narcotics, driving under the influence, or sex offenses.
c. Three (3) violations of any law regulating the sale, manufacture, and/or distribution of alcoholic beverages.
d. Five (5) violations of any municipal ordinance, except traffic violations.
(2) Within the ten (10) years immediately prior to filing:
a. Two (2) felonies.
b. Two (2) violations of any law regulating gambling, narcotics, driving under the influence, or sex offenses.

244:
(a) Retail package liquor store. No license shall be issued to any retail package liquor store where the place of business of the licensee is located within one hundred (100) yards of any public library; within one hundred (100) yards of any place of worship; or within two hundred (200) yards from any property line of any school ground or college campus.
